status: proposed for port (Builder); replaces targets.json curve for the Modeled stimulus item
disclaimer: A model for comparing plans, not a measurement of growth or recovery.

evidence_tags.evidence: Evidence-based: the number or shape comes from a cited peer-reviewed study or meta-analysis.
evidence_tags.extrapolated: Extrapolated: pooled or neighbouring evidence stretched to a muscle, level or range the studies did not measure directly.
evidence_tags.modeled: Modeled: a planning convention chosen by Coach. Not measured; adjust to how you actually respond.

schoenfeld2017.cite: Schoenfeld, Ogborn & Krieger (2017). Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Sports Sciences 35(11):1073-1082.
schoenfeld2017.used_for: Graded dose-response: <5, 5-9 and 10+ weekly sets all grew, 10+ most. Supports a curve that rises from zero with no hard floor and that the minimum is where useful growth starts, not where growth begins at all.

pelland2025.cite: Pelland et al. The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains. Sports Medicine (online Dec 2025). Earlier version: SportRxiv preprint 2024 (not peer-reviewed), doi 10.51224/srxiv.460.
pelland2025.used_for: 67 studies. Counting indirect sets as 0.5 ("fractional") fit best. Hypertrophy keeps rising with weekly volume with diminishing returns; best-fit hypertrophy model was a square-root curve. Basis for the square-root curve shape and for keeping ~0.5 credit on indirect sets.

bazvalle2022.cite: Baz-Valle, Balsalobre-Fernandez, Alix-Fages & Santos-Concejero (2022). A Systematic Review of the Effects of Different Resistance Training Volumes on Muscle Hypertrophy. Journal of Human Kinetics 81:199-210.
bazvalle2022.used_for: Trained young men: 12-20 weekly sets per muscle a reasonable range; >20 no clear extra gain for quads and biceps (triceps an exception, with pressing counted). Basis for 12-18/20 sweet spots and the ~20 diminishing-returns point on big muscles.

robinson2024.cite: Robinson, Pelland, Remmert, Refalo, Jukic, Steele & Zourdos (2024). Exploring the Dose-Response Relationship Between Estimated Resistance Training Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions. Sports Medicine 54(9):2209-2231.
robinson2024.used_for: Hypertrophy increases as sets end closer to failure (negative slope per estimated RIR); exploratory, RIR estimated, exact shape unclear. Basis for discounting sets with more reps in reserve; the specific multipliers are extrapolated/modeled.

refalo2023.cite: Refalo, Helms, Trexler, Hamilton & Fyfe (2023). Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine 53(3):649-665.
refalo2023.used_for: Failure vs non-failure gave similar hypertrophy when volume was equated. Supports full credit at 0-2 RIR (no bonus for failure).

refalo2024.cite: Refalo, Helms, Robinson, Hamilton & Fyfe (2024). Similar muscle hypertrophy following eight weeks of resistance training to momentary muscular failure or with repetitions-in-reserve in resistance-trained individuals. Journal of Sports Sciences 42(1):85-101.
refalo2024.used_for: Quads: failure vs 1-2 RIR gave the same growth; failure caused more acute fatigue. Supports multiplier 1.0 through RIR 2 and a failure surcharge on recovery, not on stimulus.

moran2017.cite: Moran-Navarro et al. (2017). Time course of recovery following resistance training leading or not to failure. European Journal of Applied Physiology.
moran2017.used_for: Trained men, bench and squat: non-failure protocols recovered mechanical performance faster between 24 and 48 h; failure slowed recovery by up to 24-48 h, some markers still off at 72 h. Anchors the 24-72 h range and the failure factor.

cheung2003.cite: Cheung, Hume & Maxwell (2003). Delayed onset muscle soreness: treatment strategies and performance factors. Sports Medicine 33(2):145-164.
cheung2003.used_for: Soreness after unaccustomed, eccentric-heavy work rises within 24 h and peaks around 24-72 h. Basis for the stretch/eccentric factor and the 96 h clamp.

mchugh2003.cite: McHugh (2003). Recent advances in the understanding of the repeated bout effect. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 13(2):88-97.
mchugh2003.used_for: Repeated exposure protects against damage from the same work. Basis for the beginner recovery factor (less protection on novel work); the 1.15 value is modeled.

schoenfeld2016rest.cite: Schoenfeld, Pope, Benik et al. (2016). Longer Interset Rest Periods Enhance Muscle Strength and Hypertrophy in Resistance-Trained Men. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 30(7):1805-1812.
schoenfeld2016rest.used_for: 3 min beat 1 min rest on compound lifts for trained men. Supports ~3 min rest for primary lifts at intermediate/advanced.

singer2024rest.cite: Singer, Wolf, Generoso et al. (2024). Give it a rest: a systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis on the effect of inter-set rest interval duration on muscle hypertrophy. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 6:1429789.
singer2024rest.used_for: Small advantage for resting >60 s; no clear extra hypertrophy benefit beyond ~90 s. Supports 1.5 min isolation rest at every level.

rp_landmarks.cite: Renaissance Periodization: Israetel, Hoffmann & Smith, Scientific Principles of Hypertrophy Training (2021) and RP "training volume landmarks" articles (MV/MEV/MAV/MRV).
rp_landmarks.used_for: PRACTITIONER, NOT PEER-REVIEWED. The three-zone idea (minimum effective, adaptive sweet spot, recoverable maximum) and the low direct minimum for front delts and traps given pressing/pulling. Used for zone structure and small-muscle sweet spots only; no RP number is copied as evidence. Note RP counts direct sets only; our zones are in fractional effective sets.

remmert2025session.cite: Remmert, Pelland, Robinson, Hinson & Zourdos (2025). Is There Too Much of a Good Thing? Meta-Regressions of the Effect of Per-Session Volume on Hypertrophy and Strength. SportRxiv PREPRINT (not peer-reviewed); conference abstract in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 2025.
remmert2025session.used_for: PREPRINT. Hypertrophy rises with per-session volume with diminishing returns from the start; best-fit hypertrophy model linear-log; point of undetectable outcome superiority ~11 fractional sets per session (more sets still added a little, with a much smaller slope and wide uncertainty; too little data at very high per-session volumes). Reports an unpublished analysis by Krieger finding diminishing returns above 6-8 total sets per session with >= 2 min rest (not verified by us; unpublished). Basis for the per-session knee near 8-12 sets for a large muscle.

schoenfeld2019freq.cite: Schoenfeld, Grgic & Krieger (2019). How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the effects of resistance training frequency. Journal of Sports Sciences 37(11):1286-1295.
schoenfeld2019freq.used_for: With weekly volume equated, training a muscle 1 vs 2+ days a week gave similar hypertrophy. Keeps the per-session penalty small: splitting the same weekly sets should change the model only modestly.

macdougall1995.cite: MacDougall, Gibala, Tarnopolsky, MacDonald, Interisano & Yarasheski (1995). The time course for elevated muscle protein synthesis following heavy resistance exercise. Canadian Journal of Applied Physiology 20(4):480-486.
macdougall1995.used_for: In trained young men, biceps muscle protein synthesis was ~50% higher at 4 h and ~109% higher at 24 h after 12 sets to failure, and back to within ~14% of the control arm (not significant) by ~36 h. Basis for "the growth signal from one session lasts roughly 1-2 days in trained lifters".

damas2016.cite: Damas, Phillips, Libardi, Vechin, Lixandrao, Jannig, et al. (2016). Resistance training-induced changes in integrated myofibrillar protein synthesis are related to hypertrophy only after attenuation of muscle damage. Journal of Physiology 594(18):5209-5222.
damas2016.used_for: Measured integrated myofibrillar protein synthesis over 0-48 h after a session at weeks 1, 3 and 10 of training; once damage had subsided (weeks 3 and 10) the 0-48 h response correlated with hypertrophy (r ~0.9). Supports a 48 h window as the relevant post-session period in trained muscle.

schoenfeld2016freq.cite: Schoenfeld, Ogborn & Krieger (2016). Effects of resistance training frequency on measures of muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine 46(11):1689-1697.
schoenfeld2016freq.used_for: Training a muscle twice a week gave larger hypertrophy effect sizes than once a week (0.49 vs 0.30; 10 studies). The later, larger volume-equated analysis (Schoenfeld 2019) found frequency mattered little when weekly sets are equal, so "too long a gap" is an info note, not a warning.

zones.unit: weekly effective sets (after credit rules and the per-session discount)

definition.min: Minimum: where the model's growth zone starts (= targets.json min x levelMinFactor; same blue/green edge as today). Sets below it still count.
definition.sweet_lo..sweet_hi: Sweet spot: the range the model favours for this muscle and level.
definition.diminishing: Diminishing-returns point (= targets.json max; amber starts above it, same as rules.json volume_bands). Past it, extra sets add little modeled stimulus for their recovery cost.

level_rule.sweet: intermediate sweet spot x {"beginner": [0.75, 0.85], "intermediate": [1.0, 1.0], "advanced": [1.0, 1.0]} (lo, hi), kept above min+1 and at least 2 wide

chest.note: Large muscle; studied mostly through bench-type pressing in pooled data.

front_delts.note: Gets most of its work from pressing (credited at the discounted secondary rate). Direct front-delt work is rarely needed once pressing is in the plan.

traps.note: Gets indirect work from rows, deadlifts and shrug-like pulls.

triceps.note: Baz-Valle 2022 found >20 sets helped triceps when pressing was counted; the model keeps 18 as the point where returns flatten.

curve.replaces: targets.json curve (S = 1 - exp(-x/k), k = level min / ln 2.5)
curve.formula: c = D/45; x <= D: S = ln(1 + x/c) / ln(1 + D/c) / 1.1  (= 0.909 at D);  x > D: S = (1 + 0.1*(1 - exp(-(x-D)/tau))) / 1.1, tau = 0.1 * (c + D) * ln(1 + D/c) (slope-continuous);  D = zones diminishing point (targets.max)
curve.reads_as: share of this muscle's modeled plateau (100% = plateau). Same shape for every muscle relative to its own diminishing-returns point D (c = D/45): 91% at D, ~70% at 0.4 x D, ~79% at 0.6 x D, ~89% at 0.9 x D. Percentages compare within one muscle only.

tags.shape: modeled (vol5: log shape picked by Mr Dude and tuned to his anchors 70% at 8 / ~91% at 20 for chest; concave diminishing returns are evidence-based (Pelland 2025), but Pelland's best-fit weekly model was square root, not log; see fit_vs_evidence)
tags.plateau_beyond_D: modeled (Baz-Valle 2022: no clear extra gain >20 sets for quads/biceps)

per_set.formula: per set n: 1/(1 + (n-1)/c); workout stimulus = sum over its effective sets (fractional last set pro rata); c = 0.4 x targets.json session.muscles[m].heavy

smooth_vol5.formula: s <= a: g = s; s > a: g = a + b ln(1 + (s - a)/b); a = 0.8 x H, b = 0.4 x H, H = targets.json session.muscles[m].heavy

session_discount.legacy: cap/factor = the pre-vol5 hard cut (10 sets, then 50%); kept only so an unported client still runs.
session_discount.tag: modeled (log shape per Remmert 2025 PREPRINT; c fitted to its ~11-set anchor)

curve.fit_vs_evidence: Pelland et al. (Sports Medicine 2025) compared 7 functional forms for fractional weekly sets vs hypertrophy (linear, spline, linear-log, polynomial, square root, quadratic, reciprocal) with a BIC-approximated Bayes factor and picked square root as the best fit; the paper does not print the margin over linear-log in the main text, so we cannot say how close the log fit was, and the authors state the data remain compatible with multiple functional forms, with few studies above ~25 weekly sets. Their efficiency tiers (minimum effective dose 4 sets; 5-10 higher, 11-18 intermediate, 19-29 lower efficiency) describe per-set efficiency, not a share of a ceiling. Scaled so both read 91% at 20 sets, Pelland's square-root point estimate puts 8 sets at ~58% and 12-18 at ~70-86%; the active log curve puts 8 at 70% and 12-18 at ~79-89%, i.e. it front-loads low volumes more than Pelland's point estimate. That is a coaching choice (Mr Dude's anchors), not a better fit. The per-session preprint (Remmert 2025) did find linear-log best for per-session volume. No study measures "% of plateau", so the percentages are a display convention.

input.x_dec: sum over the week's workouts of the per-set-decayed workout stimulus (session.credit)
input.x_equiv: the raw weekly sets x such that 2 x g(x/2) = x_dec (g = session.credit for that muscle); solve by bisection (monotone)
input.weekly_pct: curve.formula(x_equiv, D) with D = zones diminishing
input.why: The log weekly curve was tuned by Mr Dude in raw weekly sets (chest 8 -> 70%, 12-18 -> 80-89%, 20 -> 91%). Feeding it decayed sets directly discounted twice. Mapping the decayed total back to its 2-sessions-a-week raw equivalent keeps his anchors exactly for an even 2x split; other layouts move relative to that (one heavy session lower, 3 light sessions slightly higher).
input.zones_and_colours: stay on raw weekly effective sets (familiar set-count targets, unchanged checker); only the % uses x_equiv

credit.formula: effective(set, muscle) = rating x prox(RIR_set + offset[role]); rating < 0.25 -> 0; then per-session discount

prime.rule: muscle with the exercise's highest rating (ties all prime), or rating >= 0.75

credit.rir_offset_tag: modeled (a synergist that is not the limiting muscle is further from its own failure; no study measures the offset)

planned_rir_default.note: Planner tiles carry no RIR: use these (logging-spec target RIR 1-3, isolation 0-2). Prime movers therefore score exactly as today in the planner.

credit.logged: Use set.rir (0-4, 4 = 4+). Null RIR = planned default for that exercise type (logging-spec: no RIR logged still counts).
credit.vs_current: Current: every set adds sets x rating (>= 0.25) whatever the RIR. New: prime movers unchanged at RIR 0-2; secondary movers at planned RIR get x0.9, minor movers x0.8; logged sets at RIR 3/4 lose 10%/20% (more for synergists).
credit.warnings_rounding: none (vol6): zones, colours and warnings use exact effective sets; 0.5 rounding is display-only (targets.json counting.display_round_to)
credit.tag: rating from exercises.json (modeled coaching estimates, 0.5 ~ Pelland fractional); prox 0-2 evidence, 3-4 extrapolated, 5+ modeled

recovery.recommendation: Show both: estimated recovery hours per muscle per session (for spacing) and the week against generic benchmark routines (for total load). Drop raw "pts" from the UI; keep % of saved baseline as an optional third line.
recovery.hours_formula: vol8: h = (24 + 4 x max(0, F - 2)) x (1 + 0.15 x stretch share) x size[muscle] x level; clamp 12-96 h; round to 6 h. F = recovery load = sum over that muscle's sets in the workout of credit x effort[RIR of the set] x axial[exercise].

params.axial_rule: high: heavy_squats/heavy_hinges, fatigue 1.5 or good mornings; isolation: type isolation; machine_compound: machine/smith/plate-loaded/cable compounds; free_compound: other compounds

tags.axial: modeled (classes from existing data: heavy squat/hinge lists, fatigue 1.5, equipment, type)

display.range_rule: low = hours x 0.8, high = hours x 1.2, both in half days (floor / ceil); under 20 h shows "about a day"
display.never: Do not show exact hours or "fully recovered".
display.caveat: A planning baseline. Sleep, nutrition, stress and age change real recovery.

benchmarks.metric: vol8b: week_cost = sum over the week of per-set fatigue (type_base x axial x effort at planned RIR) = the sum of the workout load points
benchmarks.display: Week load ≈ {ratio}x a {nearest}. Show the ladder of benchmarks with this week marked.

recovery.caveat: A planning baseline. Sleep, nutrition, stress and age change real recovery.

beginner.why: Newer lifters get more soreness and damage from the same work because they lack the repeated-bout protection trained muscles build (McHugh 2003). Size of the factor is modeled.

intermediate.why: Reference level the hours are calibrated on (trained lifters in Moran-Navarro 2017).

advanced.why: Repeated-bout protection is high, but heavier absolute loads add fatigue; the evidence does not show a clear net direction, so no adjustment.

assumptions: Hours are for the muscle to be ready to train hard again, not for soreness to vanish.
They assume normal sleep, eating and stress; those change real recovery and are not modeled.
Newer lifters get a 15% longer estimate; intermediate and advanced use the same baseline.
Recovery adds up set by set: each effective set beyond 2 adds about 4 hours, more if it is close to failure (RIR 0: x1.2, RIR 1: x1.1) and less if it is easy (RIR 3: x0.9, RIR 4+: x0.8).

Heavy spine-loading lifts (squats, deadlifts, good mornings) count 1.3x per set, other free-weight compounds 1.1x, machine and cable compounds 1.0x, isolation 0.9x. These weights are a modeling choice.
Stretch-heavy (eccentric) exercises add up to 15%; big muscles take 10% longer, small ones 15% less.

slope_justification.why: No study gives hours per set. Calibrated so 4 sets at RIR 2 ~ 1.5 days and 8 sets near failure ~ 2.5-3 days for a large muscle, matching 24-48 h recovery after non-failure work and up to ~72 h after failure work (Moran-Navarro 2017) and the 24-72 h soreness window (Cheung 2003).

personal_baseline.metric: week_cost from logged working sets (done sets x exercises.fatigue)
exclude: weeks with < 50% of planned working sets done
personal_baseline.why_4: Four weeks smooths normal week-to-week swings and matches the 4-week windows used by block_compare and the progress trend. Modeled.
personal_baseline.toggle: User can switch between the two at any time; the choice is saved.

tags.info/warn limits: modeled (planning convenience, not a physiological limit)

wording.message: {day} runs about {min} minutes, over the {warn_min}-minute limit for your level. Cut sets or split the day.
wording.message_info: {day} runs about {min} minutes, close to the {warn_min}-minute limit for your level. Put the big lifts first, or trim a few sets.
wording.note: vol3: written to rules.json rules[id=session_length]; replaces the unsourced "focus and output drop" text.

session_time.status: vol3: live. rules.json rules[id=session_length].by_level drives warnings in the UI and tools/check_program.py.

drops_below_min: muscles that were >= min and fall below it
schema.verdict: clean | tradeoff (tradeoff when drops_below_min is non-empty)

swaps.display: Show the swap with its fatigue delta; if verdict = tradeoff, add one line: "Drops {muscle} below its minimum ({after} of {min} sets)". Only list muscles whose delta is >= 0.5 set.

sqrt.note: vol1-vol4 active curve; shape of Pelland 2025 best-fit weekly model [E shape]. Kept for comparison.

log.formula: c = D/45; x <= D: S = ln(1 + x/c) / ln(1 + D/c) / 1.1  (= 0.909 at D);  x > D: S = (1 + 0.1*(1 - exp(-(x-D)/tau))) / 1.1, tau = 0.1 * (c + D) * ln(1 + D/c) (slope-continuous);  D = zones diminishing point (targets.max)

session.unit: effective sets in one workout for one muscle (credit rules applied)
session.credit: per set n: 1/(1 + (n-1)/c); workout stimulus = sum over its effective sets (fractional last set pro rata); c = 0.4 x targets.json session.muscles[m].heavy
session.feeds_weekly: vol8b: weekly % = curve.formula applied to x_equiv(sum over workouts of the workout stimulus): the raw sets that give the same decayed total when split evenly over 2 workouts (so Mr Dude's anchors hold for a 2x/week layout and one-heavy-session weeks read lower). Weekly zones, colours and warnings still count raw effective sets (no decay)
session.reset: Rest of >= 20 h between workouts resets the count: each day starts again at set 1 (no carryover). Justification: with weekly sets equal, spreading them over more days does not reduce growth (Schoenfeld 2019) [E], and there is no data to size a partial carryover, so none is modeled [M]. Two workouts < 20 h apart (same-day doubles) continue the count.
session.fit: Form: credit_n = 1/(1 + (n-1)/c), so the cumulative stimulus of n sets ~ c x ln((n + c - 0.5)/(c - 0.5)), a log curve (the shape Remmert 2025 found best for per-session volume; PREPRINT). c = 4 for a large muscle (0.4 x the targets.json session heavy anchor: 10 -> c 4, 8 -> c 3.2, 6 -> 2.4, 5 -> 2). Chosen so a set is worth half the first by set 5, the cumulative curve bends over between 6 and 10 sets, and set 11 is worth < 0.3 of set 1, matching the preprint's ~11 fractional sets beyond which more volume was not detectably better. The preprint does not publish a per-set curve, so c is a fit to those anchors, not an estimate from the data [modeled].

evidence.summary: Shape: log (Remmert 2025 PREPRINT, best-fit per-session model linear-log; ~11 fractional sets per session with no detectable further benefit). Rate c: fitted to those anchors, not estimated.

session.checker_note: junk_volume_session (warn at > 10 raw effective sets) unchanged; session_dose heavy now fires past low_return_from.

goal_notes.muscle_size: All 1: the default targets are already built for whole-body size.
goal_notes.strength: Prime movers of squat, bench, deadlift and row at 1.05-1.1; small isolation-only muscles at 0.9. Kept modest because strength comes mostly from load and practice, not volume order.
goal_notes.joint_friendly: All 1: this goal changes exercise choice and rep ranges, not which muscles get priority.
goal_notes.maintain: All 1: maintenance keeps every muscle level.
goal_notes.aesthetic_v_taper: Side delts 1.3, lats 1.25, biceps and triceps 1.2, rear delts, upper back and chest 1.1; legs 0.9. Puts width and arms first when filling sets.
goal_notes.aesthetic_lower_emphasis: Glutes 1.3, abductors 1.2, hamstrings and side delts 1.15, quads 1.1; chest, arms, forearms 0.9-0.95, traps 0.8. Puts glutes and legs first when filling sets.
goal_notes.conditioning: All 1: conditioning work changes session design, not muscle priority.

session_vol5.unit: effective sets in one session for one muscle (credit rules applied)
session_vol5.credit: s <= a: g = s; s > a: g = a + b ln(1 + (s - a)/b); a = 0.8 x H, b = 0.4 x H, H = targets.json session.muscles[m].heavy

zones.diminishing: a .. a+b (each set worth 1.0 down to 0.5)

session_vol5.feeds_weekly: weekly x = sum over days of g(day effective sets); then the weekly curve

evidence.summary: Per-session volume shows diminishing returns with a best-fit linear-log shape and an ~11 fractional-set point past which extra sets were not detectably better (Remmert 2025, PREPRINT). Frequency with volume equated made little difference (Schoenfeld 2019), so the split penalty is kept small.

session_vol5.checker_note: Program check rule junk_volume_session (threshold 10 raw effective sets) is unchanged.

workout.status: vol7 (2026-10-31) workouts first; vol8 per-set rebuild: stimulus decays set by set inside a workout and resets with rest; fatigue and recovery add up per set (effort and axial loading).

fatigue.metric: workout load points = sum over sets of type_base[type] x axial[exercise] x effort[RIR] (volume-model.json recovery.params type_base, axial_by_exercise, effort); replaces exercises.fatigue in the per-workout index

reference.name: Typical intermediate upper day
reference.source: splits.json upper-lower intermediate 4-day, mean of Upper A and Upper B

fatigue.index_formula: load_index = round(100 x load points / reference points)
fatigue.display: Fatigue bar: "{index} (100 = a typical upper-body day)" with the tier name; secondary line: "{hard_sets} hard sets, about {minutes} min".
fatigue.why: Raw points have no meaning to a user and "hard-set equivalents" would mislead (an isolation set counts 0.8, a heavy squat set 1.5). A named, familiar session pegged at 100 makes any workout readable at a glance ("about 1.3 upper days") and does not change when we tune exercise ratings. The plain hard-set count is shown beside it so nothing is hidden.
fatigue.tag: modeled (relative comparison; per-set weights and tiers are planning conventions)
fatigue.caveat: A planning baseline. Sleep, nutrition, stress and age change real recovery.

stimulus.per_muscle: workout stimulus g = sum of per-set credits 1/(1+(n-1)/c) over that day's effective sets (volume-model.json session); planned RIR for the proximity discount
stimulus.payout: payout_pct_of_weekly_plateau = 100 x S_week(x_week) x g_day / x_week, where x_week = sum over days of g and S_week is the active weekly curve. Read: "this workout delivers about N% of the weekly plateau for chest".
stimulus.display: Per muscle: small bar of length g, coloured by session_zone; label "+N%". Order by effective sets; show up to 6 muscles, the rest under "more".
stimulus.tag: modeled (per-set decay fitted to Remmert 2025 PREPRINT anchors; dose floor and payout split)

ready_in.formula: vol8: h = (24 + 4 x max(0, F - 2)) x (1 + 0.15 x stretch share) x size[muscle] x level; clamp 12-96 h; round to 6 h. F = recovery load = sum over that muscle's sets in the workout of credit x effort[RIR of the set] x axial[exercise].
ready_in.display: about {lo}–{hi} days (see recovery.display; never exact hours)
ready_in.computed_for: every muscle with >= 1 effective set in the workout
ready_in.caveat: A planning baseline. Sleep, nutrition, stress and age change real recovery.

gaps.meaningful_session: a session counts for spacing when that muscle gets >= targets.json session.muscles[m].light effective sets
gaps.gap: days between consecutive meaningful sessions x 24 h (same time of day assumed); the week wraps (Fri -> next Mon = 72 h)
gaps.max_gap_rule: largest gap > 120 h (6+ days) for a rules.json frequency_muscles muscle -> recovery_gap_long (info). Supersedes low_frequency in the UI for the same muscle.
gaps.evidence: One hard session raises muscle protein synthesis for roughly 24-48 h in trained lifters (MacDougall 1995: back near baseline by ~36 h; Damas 2016: the 0-48 h response tracks growth once training is established) [E]. Training a muscle about twice a week beat once a week in the 2016 frequency meta-analysis (Schoenfeld 2016) [E], but with weekly sets equal the difference largely disappears (Schoenfeld 2019) [E]. So a long gap mostly matters because it makes it harder to fit enough weekly sets in good-quality sessions. The 5-day cut-off (flag at 6+ days, i.e. effectively once a week) is a planning choice [M].
gaps.reset: Rest of >= 20 h between workouts resets the count: each day starts again at set 1 (no carryover). Justification: with weekly sets equal, spreading them over more days does not reduce growth (Schoenfeld 2019) [E], and there is no data to size a partial carryover, so none is modeled [M]. Two workouts < 20 h apart (same-day doubles) continue the count.
gaps.overlap_rule: recovery_overlap (info): a meaningful session on 3+ consecutive days, or a repeat before 0.5 x the lower edge of the previous ready-in range (0.5 x 0.8 x hours) or within 24 h. "Clearly not recovered" = less than half of the earliest ready time has passed.

workout.never: No medical claims; do not say "fully recovered" or show exact hours.

invariant.why_it_holds: per-set credit only falls within a workout and resets after >= 20 h, so the first sets of a second day are always worth at least the last sets of a long single workout.
